opus-5.5.text:
I think the people who get the most out of it are the ones who treat the AI less like an autocomplete and more like a teammate they're delegating to. That's a real shift in mindset. The most successful users I see are really good at breaking a problem down, giving clear context about what they want and why, and then letting the agent run with it, rather than micromanaging every line.

A big part of it is also being comfortable working in parallel. Instead of sitting and watching one task finish, they'll kick off several things at once, maybe one agent is fixing a bug, another is writing tests, another is exploring a refactor, and then they come back and review. Your role starts to look more like a tech lead: you're setting direction, reviewing output, and deciding what to merge.

And I'd say the other piece is investing in the environment. People who have good tests, clear documentation in the repo, and a codebase that's easy to navigate get dramatically better results, because the model can verify its own work and find its way around. It's the same things that make a codebase good for a new human engineer, it just pays off even more now.

Finally, there's a bit of curiosity and willingness to experiment. The capabilities are changing quickly, so the people who keep pushing, trying harder tasks, and updating their sense of what's possible tend to pull ahead. If you tried something six months ago and it didn't work, it's worth trying again.

r001.rationale: The response mentions breaking down problems, reviewing output, and maintaining a good codebase, but does not identify software engineering fundamentals as a contributor to success.

r002.rationale: The response discusses setting direction and having a navigable codebase, but does not advocate using AI within a deliberately planned software architecture.

r003.rationale: The response recommends reviewing AI output, but does not state that understanding the code enables developers to go further than they could without that understanding.

fable-5.1.text:
I think the biggest thing is a shift in mindset. The people who get the most out of it stop thinking of themselves as the person who types every line, and start thinking of themselves as the person who decides what should exist and whether it's right. That sounds small, but it changes everything about how you work.

Concretely, a few things stand out. First, they're really good at describing intent. Not just "fix this bug," but what the system is supposed to do, what the constraints are, what they've already tried, what "done" looks like. The more context you give the model about the actual goal, the less it has to guess, and most failures I see are really failures of under-specification rather than the model not being capable.

Second, they verify. They treat the output the way they'd treat a pull request from a talented new teammate: probably good, but you still read it, you still run the tests, you still ask "why did you do it this way?" The people who get burned are usually the ones who either trust it blindly or distrust it so much they never delegate anything meaningful.

Third, they decompose well. They know how to break a big ambiguous problem into chunks that are well-scoped enough to hand off, and they build in checkpoints. That's honestly just good engineering, but AI rewards it more than ever, because a well-scoped task is one the model can actually finish end to end.

And the last thing, which I think is underrated, is curiosity. The people who are most successful are the ones who keep experimenting with what they can hand over. Six months ago they wouldn't have trusted it with a refactor across the codebase, now they try it, see where it breaks, and adjust. The capabilities are moving fast enough that your mental model of what's possible goes stale quickly, so the willingness to keep re-testing your own assumptions matters a lot.

r001.rationale: The response mentions verification and decomposition as good engineering practices, but does not identify a strong grounding in software engineering fundamentals as a contributor to success.

r002.rationale: It advocates breaking work into scoped chunks and adding checkpoints, but does not say to use AI within a deliberately planned software architecture.

r003.rationale: It says developers should read and verify AI output, but does not state that understanding the generated code lets them go further than they could without that understanding.

astra-6.text:
I think the biggest thing is being clear about what you’re trying to accomplish, and then being willing to iterate. You don’t need to specify every detail up front, but you do need some way to tell whether the result is good. What should the software do? What would you test? What constraints matter?

And then stay curious about what the AI produces. Ask it to explain a decision, look at the changes, give it feedback when something isn’t right. You can move very quickly, but you still want to build an understanding of the thing you’re making. That combination—a clear goal, fast feedback, and curiosity—is really powerful.

r001.rationale: The response emphasizes clear goals, testing, constraints, and feedback, but does not identify software engineering fundamentals as a contributor to success.

r002.rationale: It does not advocate planning or using AI within a software architecture.

r003.rationale: It encourages understanding what is being built, but does not state that understanding AI-written code enables developers to go further than they otherwise could.

sol-6.1.text:
I think the biggest thing is being clear about what you’re trying to accomplish and giving the model a way to check its work. That doesn’t mean you need to specify every line of code. It means explaining the goal, the constraints, and what success looks like.

Then it’s an iterative process. You try something, look at the result, run the tests, and give feedback. If something goes wrong, bring the actual error back into the conversation. The people who do this well stay engaged: they ask questions, challenge assumptions, and make sure they understand the important decisions.

And I’d encourage people to experiment. Start with something small enough that you can tell whether it worked, then gradually hand over larger tasks as you learn where the model needs guidance.

r001.rationale: The response recommends testing and providing feedback, but does not identify strong software engineering fundamentals as a contributor to success.

r002.rationale: It discusses explaining goals and constraints, but does not advocate using AI within a deliberately planned software architecture.

r003.rationale: It advises understanding important decisions, but does not say that understanding AI-written code enables developers to go further than they otherwise could.
